Maths at work

Construction and the built environment

Jobs in this route, and the maths they use.

Ratio

Bricklayer

Construction and the built environment

\(0.3 \div 6 = 0.05\) m³ per part

Concrete for a shed base is often mixed \(1 : 2 : 3\): 1 part cement, 2 parts sand, 3 parts gravel, in buckets of the same size. You need 0.3 m³ of dry mix.

  1. Total parts: \(1 + 2 + 3 = 6\).
  2. One part: \(0.3 \div 6 = 0.05\) m³.
  3. Cement 0.05 m³, sand 0.10 m³, gravel 0.15 m³.

Percentages

Plumber

Construction and the built environment

\(\pounds 350 \times 1.2 = \pounds 420\)

A VAT-registered plumber adds 20% VAT to the bill. To add 20%, multiply by 1.2. The job costs £350 before VAT.

  1. \(\pounds 350 \times 1.2 = \pounds 420\).
  2. The VAT is £70.

Electrician

Construction and the built environment

\(5.4 \div 230 \times 100 = 2.3\%\)

Voltage drops along a long cable. The wiring rules (BS 7671) allow at most 3% on a lighting circuit and 5% on others. The UK supply is 230 V.

  1. Most allowed on lighting: \(3\% \text{ of } 230 = 0.03 \times 230 = 6.9\) V.
  2. A lighting circuit drops 5.4 V. As a percentage: \(5.4 \div 230 \times 100 = 2.3\%\).
  3. 2.3% is under 3%, so it passes.

Self-employed plasterer

Construction and the built environment

\(0.2 \times 19430 = \pounds 3{,}886\) to set aside

Uses example figures: the numbers marked (example figure) or (example figures) are made up to show the method.

No boss takes tax off for you, so you set money aside yourself. Same 2026 to 2027 rules: £12,570 tax-free, then 20%. This year's profit is £32,000 (example figure). National Insurance comes on top.

  1. Taxed: \(32000 - 12570 = \pounds 19{,}430\).
  2. Income tax: \(0.2 \times 19430 = \pounds 3{,}886\).

Area and perimeter

Painter and decorator

Construction and the built environment

\(64 \div 16 = 4\) litres

Uses example figures: the numbers marked (example figure) or (example figures) are made up to show the method.

A room is 4 m by 3.5 m, with walls 2.5 m high. There is a 2 m² door and a 3.5 m² window. Two coats; the tin says 1 litre covers 16 m² (example figure).

  1. Perimeter: \(4 + 3.5 + 4 + 3.5 = 15\) m.
  2. Wall area: \(15 \times 2.5 = 37.5\) m².
  3. Take away door and window: \(37.5 - 5.5 = 32\) m².
  4. Two coats: 64 m². Paint: \(64 \div 16 = 4\) litres.

Angles

Wall and floor tiler

Construction and the built environment

\(3 \times 120 = 360^\circ \)

Tiles fit with no gaps only if the angles meeting at each corner add up to 360°.

  1. A regular hexagon's angle: \((6 - 2) \times 180 \div 6 = 120^\circ \). Three meet: \(3 \times 120 = 360^\circ \), so they fit.
  2. Octagon and square floors: \((8 - 2) \times 180 \div 8 = 135^\circ \), and \(135 + 135 + 90 = 360^\circ \).
  3. A regular pentagon's angle is 108°: \(360 \div 108 = 3.33\), not a whole number, so gaps.

Gradients

Highways engineer

Construction and the built environment

\(1000 \times 0.10 = 100\) m climb

A steep-hill sign shows the gradient as a percentage: 10% is 1 in 10 (1 m up for every 10 m along).

  1. Over 1 km at 10%: \(1000 \times 0.10 = 100\) m of height.
  2. 20% is \(1 \div 0.2 = 1\) in 5, twice as steep.

Architectural technician

Construction and the built environment

\(2000 \div 12 = 166.7\) mm

Building regulations set how steep a wheelchair ramp may be. The shorter the ramp, the steeper it is allowed: \(1 : 12\) for a 2 m ramp, \(1 : 20\) for 10 m.

  1. 2 m ramp: \(2000 \div 12 = 166.7\) mm, so the rise can be at most 166 mm (round down: it's a maximum).
  2. 10 m ramp: \(10000 \div 20 = 500\) mm.

Transformations

Painter and decorator

Construction and the built environment

\(64 \div 2 = 32\) cm drop

A "half drop" wallpaper's pattern is translated down by half its repeat on every other strip. A 64 cm pattern repeat (the manufacturer's example):

  1. The next strip moves down \(64 \div 2 = 32\) cm.
